source.title: Full-Length Machining Process of a Falcon on the DMU 85 H-monoBLOCK
source.transcript_note: No auto-generated or manual subtitles available. Knowledge extracted from video description, chapter markers, key facts overlay, and visual analysis of machining operations.

machine.design: monoBLOCK single-casting construction for maximum rigidity

kinematics.description: Horizontal spindle orientation with A/C trunnion table. The H designation means horizontal chip evacuation, ideal for long unattended cuts on parts generating heavy chips.
advantages: Gravity-assisted chip evacuation (chips fall away from workpiece)
Better coolant drainage from work zone
Superior surface finish on complex 3D forms
Ideal for long unattended machining cycles like this 70-hour falcon

axis_travels.note: DMU 85 series indicates 850mm primary travel. H-monoBLOCK has generous Z for deep-cavity 5-axis work.

spindle.note: speedMASTER spindle standard. Optional 20,000 RPM or 40,000 RPM spindles available.

tool_changer.note: 63 tool changes documented in this falcon job, well within standard 60-tool magazine (some tools used for multiple operations)

part.name: Falcon sculpture/demo part
part.description: Highly detailed bird of prey (falcon) with outstretched wings, intricate feather details, head with beak, legs with talons, and rootstock/perch base. This is a showpiece demonstrating full 5-axis simultaneous capability.

material.temper: T6 or T651 (implied by machining application)

properties.machinability: Good. ISO N-group, relatively free-cutting for a high-strength aluminum. Produces long stringy chips at aggressive feeds, segmented chips at moderate feeds.

machining_notes: Excellent choice for complex demo part — machines well at high speeds
kc1.1 ~ 700 MPa (canonical PRISM ISO N-group value)
Supports high RPM strategies (10,000-15,000 RPM typical for 5-axis sculpting)
Requires sharp tools and proper chip evacuation to avoid re-cutting
Built-up edge (BUE) risk at low speeds — stay above 150 m/min cutting speed
Horizontal spindle orientation of DMU 85 H aids chip evacuation during 70-hour cycle

part.estimated_dimensions_mm: Approximately 400x300x250 based on DMU 85 H table size and falcon proportions

features: Feather texture detail across entire wing surfaces
Thin wing tips requiring careful approach strategy
Complex head geometry with beak and eye detail
Undercut areas between wings and body
Legs with talons — thin cylindrical features
Tail feather underside — difficult access angle

process_summary.methodology: Progressive roughing strategy with multiple orientations, followed by targeted semi-finishing and finishing passes. The falcon is machined from a single billet with no re-fixturing visible, taking advantage of the A/C trunnion to access all surfaces from the top fixturing.

order_of_operations.strategy: 3+2 indexed roughing with high-feed face mill or large-diameter end mill. Material removed from top of billet to define wing profile from above. Likely adaptive/trochoidal roughing strategy for high MRR.
order_of_operations.notes: First operation establishes primary wing surfaces from top access. Longest single roughing pass at 4 minutes of video time (~5.5 hours estimated real time).

order_of_operations.strategy: Indexed approach with smaller end mill to access wing tip geometry. Multiple table rotations visible to access thin, tapered wing tip features.
order_of_operations.notes: Wing tips require careful approach — thin walls developing early in the process.

order_of_operations.strategy: Tilted approach to rough falcon head profile. Spherical geometry requires multiple indexed orientations.
order_of_operations.notes: Head is complex 3D form — beak, eye socket, crest features defined in rough.

order_of_operations.strategy: Slot-type roughing between wing surfaces to separate wing forms from body mass. Likely long-reach end mill.
order_of_operations.notes: Short operation — clearing material between the two wing surfaces. Deep pocket between wings.

order_of_operations.strategy: Table rotated to present front of falcon. Roughing chest, lower body, and frontal wing surfaces. Multiple depth passes with end mill.
order_of_operations.notes: Major reorientation — accessing front/chest of falcon. Shows versatility of horizontal 5-axis layout.

order_of_operations.strategy: Table tilted/rotated to access wing surfaces from side approach. Likely uses A-axis tilt with C-axis rotation for optimal tool engagement.
order_of_operations.notes: Side approach to wing surfaces. Important for reaching undercut regions beneath wing surfaces.

order_of_operations.strategy: A-axis tilted to access wing undersides. Material removed from below the wing plane.
order_of_operations.notes: Accessing bottom surfaces of wings — demonstrates full 5-axis envelope utilization.

order_of_operations.strategy: Smaller diameter tool to clear material left by larger roughing tool in wing tip areas. Pencil-tracing or rest-machining strategy following previous tool boundary.
order_of_operations.notes: First rest-roughing pass. Critical for reducing semi-finishing load on delicate wing tip geometry.

order_of_operations.strategy: Ball end mill or bull-nose end mill with moderate stepover (likely 10-15% of tool diameter). Leaves uniform 0.2-0.5mm stock for finishing.
order_of_operations.notes: First semi-finish pass. Transitions to simultaneous 5-axis for smooth, uniform stock preparation.

order_of_operations.strategy: Small ball end mill with fine stepover for scallop-controlled surface finish. Simultaneous 5-axis to maintain optimal tool engagement angle.
order_of_operations.notes: Note: Video description shows same timestamp as semi-finishing (23:19). The finishing operation for wing tips blends into the next roughing body operation. Fine scallop height control for feather detail.

order_of_operations.operation: Roughing body (labeled as 'Finishing wing tips' continuation + rest roughing wings)
order_of_operations.strategy: Primary body roughing — removing bulk material from falcon torso. Large-diameter end mill for MRR.
order_of_operations.notes: Video description lists 'Roughing body' at 23:19 as a separate chapter. Body roughing happens after wing tips are finished to avoid damaging delicate features.

order_of_operations.strategy: Smaller tools following contours left by previous roughing passes on wing surfaces. Multiple orientations for complete coverage.
order_of_operations.notes: Extensive rest roughing phase — 4 minutes of video time. Cleaning up all wing surfaces before semi-finishing.

order_of_operations.strategy: Ball end mill semi-finish across entire falcon body. Uniform stock left for final finishing pass.
order_of_operations.notes: Global semi-finish after all roughing and rest-roughing of main body complete.

order_of_operations.strategy: Roughing the perch/base that the falcon stands on. Organic tree-stump shape requires freeform machining.
order_of_operations.notes: Rootstock is machined after main falcon body to maintain rigidity of stock during critical operations.

order_of_operations.strategy: Smaller tool to clean up rootstock geometry. Short operation.
order_of_operations.notes: Quick cleanup of rootstock before finishing begins on main falcon body.

order_of_operations.strategy: High-quality surface finish pass across main falcon body. Small ball end mill (likely 4-8mm diameter) with fine stepover for scallop control. Simultaneous 5-axis maintains constant tool-to-surface angle.
order_of_operations.notes: Primary finishing pass. This is where the feather detail, body contours, and head features achieve final surface quality. Tool lead/tilt angle carefully controlled for optimal surface finish.

order_of_operations.strategy: Clearing remaining material from bottom/underside of part. A-axis tilted significantly to access undersurfaces.
order_of_operations.notes: Long rest-roughing phase for difficult-to-reach bottom areas. The horizontal spindle orientation is advantageous here as chips fall away from the cutting zone.

order_of_operations.strategy: Finishing the underside of the tail feathers — extremely complex geometry requiring simultaneous 5-axis with optimal tool lead angles to avoid gouging.
order_of_operations.notes: Complex access angle required. Tail feathers are thin, detailed features machined from below. Long-reach tooling likely required.

order_of_operations.strategy: Clearing material between and around falcon legs. Small diameter tools in confined spaces. Multiple tool changes likely for progressive size reduction.
order_of_operations.notes: Longest single chapter in the video (5 minutes). The legs are thin cylindrical features with talons — the inter-leg space is a deep, narrow cavity requiring careful tool selection and collision avoidance.

order_of_operations.strategy: Final detailed rest roughing of rootstock/perch base. Progressively smaller tools to define organic bark/wood texture details.
order_of_operations.notes: Extended rest roughing — rootstock has complex organic texture requiring multiple tool passes with decreasing diameter.

order_of_operations.strategy: Final finishing pass on legs, talons, and rootstock. Smallest tools used in the entire job. Fine ball end mill for maximum detail.
order_of_operations.notes: Final operation. Produces finished surfaces on the most delicate features — legs, talons, and rootstock texture.

machining_strategy_analysis.overall_approach: Progressive roughing from large to small features, followed by targeted semi-finishing and finishing. The strategy is designed to maintain maximum workpiece rigidity by leaving bulk material connected as long as possible.

phases: Phase 1 (Steps 1-7): Primary roughing from all major orientations — top, tips, head, front, sides, bottom
Phase 2 (Steps 8, 12, 14-15, 17): Rest roughing with progressively smaller tools
Phase 3 (Steps 19-20): Final rest roughing of confined areas (legs, rootstock)
roughing_strategy.key_principle: Roughing proceeds from least-constrained to most-constrained geometry. Wings first (large surfaces, easy access), then body, then rootstock, then legs (most constrained).
roughing_strategy.orientation_count: At least 7 distinct 3+2 orientations used during roughing phases

estimated_tools.primary_roughing: 16-25mm flat end mill or high-feed mill
estimated_tools.rest_roughing_small: 3-6mm end mill or ball end mill
estimated_tools.rest_roughing_detail: 1-3mm end mill for legs and tight features

semi_finishing_strategy.method: Ball end mill or bull-nose end mill with moderate stepover
semi_finishing_strategy.purpose: Create uniform stock allowance (typically 0.2-0.5mm) for finishing

finishing_strategy.method: Small ball end mill with fine stepover for scallop height control
finishing_strategy.axis_mode: Full simultaneous 5-axis for optimal tool engagement angle

key_parameters.scallop_height_control: Scallop height likely 5-15 microns for showpiece quality
key_parameters.tool_lead_angle: Optimized to avoid cutting with ball tip center (zero-speed zone)
key_parameters.tool_tilt_angle: Typically 10-15 degrees lead/tilt for ball end mill finishing on 5-axis
key_parameters.stepover_percent: 3-8% of tool diameter for fine finish
estimated_tool_diameters_mm: 2mm or 1mm ball for finest detail (talons, eye)

finishing_strategy.surface_finish_target: Ra 0.4-1.6 um typical for aluminum showpiece demo parts
strategies_used: Parallel/lace pattern on large open surfaces (wings)
Flow-line following for feather pattern direction
Pencil tracing for internal corners and blend radii

indexed_3plus2.used_for: All roughing operations (Steps 1-7) and most rest roughing
advantages: Higher rigidity — no simultaneous axis motion during cutting
Higher MRR — can push harder with locked rotary axes
Smooth continuous toolpath — no faceting at orientation boundaries
Optimal tool engagement angle maintained throughout
Can machine complex undercuts and re-entrant geometry
Better surface finish — no cusps at orientation transitions

tooling_analysis.unique_tools_estimated: 40-50 (some tools used for multiple operations across different orientations)

tool_categories.type: Solid carbide end mills, likely 3-4 flute for aluminum
tool_categories.usage: Steps 1-7 primary roughing, progressive size reduction

tool_categories.coating: Uncoated or DLC for aluminum finish quality

tool_categories.type: Tapered ball end mills, extended-reach holders
tool_categories.usage: Deep cavity access — between wings, under tail, between legs

tool_categories.type: Conical tools, lollipop cutters, or undercutting tools
tool_categories.usage: Undercuts beneath wings, between legs, rootstock detail

holder_types_estimated: Shrink-fit holders (majority — for maximum runout accuracy on finishing tools)

phase_breakdown_estimated.note: Estimated from video chapter durations, assuming time-lapse is roughly proportional to actual machining time.

observations: Rest roughing consumes more video time than primary roughing — reflects the progressive complexity of accessing confined geometry
70 hours is extremely long for an aluminum part — reflects the extreme detail level (200 programming hours invested)
At ~80x time-lapse factor, 1 minute of video = ~80 minutes of real machining
Tool change overhead: 63 changes x ~15 sec average = ~16 minutes total (negligible vs 70 hours)

coolant_analysis.type: Flood coolant (standard for aluminum on DMU H-monoBLOCK)
coolant_analysis.through_spindle_coolant: Available on DMU 85 H-monoBLOCK (20-80 bar TSC options)
purpose: Chip evacuation — critical for 70-hour unattended run
Temperature control — aluminum has high thermal conductivity but BUE risk
Surface finish quality — prevents re-cutting chips on finished surfaces
Tool life extension — important with 63+ tool positions
coolant_analysis.horizontal_advantage: Horizontal spindle orientation allows chips and coolant to drain away from work zone by gravity, reducing chip re-cutting and improving surface finish — a primary reason this machine was chosen for a 70-hour demo part

programming_analysis.cam_system: Likely Siemens NX or hyperMILL (DMG MORI partnership with both vendors)
programming_complexity_factors: 21 distinct machining operations with multiple sub-operations each
Collision avoidance for long-reach tools in confined spaces (between legs, under wings)
Rest machining calculations across tool size transitions
Scallop height optimization across complex freeform surfaces
Tool lead/tilt angle optimization for ball end mill finishing
Surface quality verification for showpiece-grade finish
programming_analysis.ratio_program_to_machine: 200:70 = 2.86:1 programming-to-machining ratio. High but typical for complex artistic/sculptural 5-axis work.

machine_selection: Horizontal 5-axis (H-type) is preferred for long unattended cycles due to chip evacuation
DMU 85 H-monoBLOCK should be added to PRISM machine catalog as a horizontal 5-axis option
monoBLOCK single-casting design provides rigidity needed for 70-hour continuous operation
process_planning: Progressive roughing strategy: large tools first, then rest-roughing with smaller tools — typically 3-4 size steps
Roughing order follows accessibility: most-accessible surfaces first, most-constrained last
Semi-finishing is a distinct phase — not just lighter roughing. Creates uniform stock for finishing.
Finishing order can differ from roughing order — delicate features (wing tips) finished first while still supported by surrounding stock
Rest roughing between legs was the single longest operation (5 min video = ~6.5 hours) — confined geometry is the bottleneck
tooling_insights: 63 tool changes for one part is not unusual for complex 5-axis work
Tool diameter progression for rest roughing: each successive tool should be ~60-70% of previous for optimal cleanup
Ball end mill finishing requires lead/tilt angle to avoid zero-speed zone at ball tip
Multiple ball end mill sizes needed — one size does not fit all surface regions
5axis_strategy: 3+2 for roughing, simultaneous for finishing is the standard hybrid approach for sculptural parts
Roughing at 3+2 gives ~30-50% higher MRR than simultaneous due to locked-axis rigidity
Transition from 3+2 to simultaneous should happen at semi-finishing stage
The DMU 85 H direct-drive rotary axes enable smooth simultaneous 5-axis motion needed for surface finish quality
surface_finish: Aluminum showpiece finish target: Ra 0.4-1.6 um
Scallop height on 5-axis ball mill finish is controlled by stepover, tool diameter, and local surface curvature
Flow-line toolpath following the direction of feather pattern enhances visual quality
Horizontal spindle reduces re-cut chip marks on finished surfaces

machine_to_add.note: Currently not in PRISM machine enrichment catalog. Should be added alongside existing DMU 50/65/80/100/125/160/200 entries.
